lead: A fuselage in flight is a thin-walled tube doing two jobs at once: it holds cabin pressure and it bends like a beam. The tail unit hangs off the rear end and feeds bending and twist into that beam. Stress analysis asks one question at every point: what stresses meet there, and do they pass the material's failure check? The same arithmetic sizes a window surround, a frame at a wing joint, and a fin root fitting. It is used in every structural repair and every mass-saving change on an aircraft.
prereq: You need: bending moment and shear ideas from Chapter 1.9, and the roles of skin, frames and longerons from Chapter 1.3.

sections.h3: The fuselage as a pressure tube and a beam

blocks.text: Cabin pressure p is a differential pressure: inside absolute pressure minus outside ambient pressure. It pushes the skin outward in all directions. On a thin circular cylinder of mean radius r and thickness t, the skin carries two membrane stresses at right angles. Hoop stress acts around the circumference: σ_h = p r / t. Longitudinal stress acts along the axis: σ_l = p r / (2t). p is in Pa, r and t in m, stresses in Pa. Hoop stress is twice longitudinal stress, so a fatigue crack usually runs along the axis, where hoop stress tries to open it.
σ_h = p r / t    σ_l = p r / (2t)
blocks.where: σ_h is hoop stress in Pa; σ_l is longitudinal stress in Pa; p is cabin differential pressure in Pa; r is mean skin radius in m; t is skin thickness in m.

blocks.text: The same tube is a beam. Bending moment M at a section produces axial stress σ_b = M y / I. M is in N·m, y is the distance from the neutral axis to the point in m, and I is second moment of area in m⁴. For a thin circular tube of mean radius r and thickness t, I ≈ π r³ t. For the thin skin the outer fibre is at y = r, so y is taken as the mean radius in the section check. Longerons and stringers add area far from the neutral axis, so the real I comes from the section idealisation, not the skin alone. The skin also carries shear between frames and longerons; shear flow is Unit 5. See Chapter 1.1 for load paths and Chapter 1.9 for how M varies.

sections.h3: Combining stresses and local load paths

blocks.text: At a point on the skin, hoop stress and longitudinal stress act on perpendicular faces. They do not add like two pulls on the same rope. The correct check combines them. For a ductile aluminium alloy, use von Mises: σ_vm = √(σ_l,total² − σ_l,total σ_h + σ_h²). The total longitudinal stress is the pressure part plus the bending part at that point: σ_l,total = p r/(2t) ± M y/I. The sign depends on whether bending puts that side in tension or compression. Compare σ_vm with the design allowable; for compression, check buckling separately in Unit 6.

blocks.where: σ_vm is von Mises equivalent stress in Pa; σ_l,total is the longitudinal stress including pressure and bending in Pa; σ_h is hoop stress in Pa.

blocks.text: Frames are rings that hold the shape and take concentrated loads: floor beams, wing attachment, landing gear, door stops. A frame spreads a local push into ring shear and bending, so the skin is not asked to carry a point load alone. A pressure bulkhead closes the pressurised cabin and turns pressure into edge shear on the shell; a domed bulkhead carries pressure mainly in membrane action, while a flat bulkhead bends. A cut-out such as a window or door removes skin area and breaks the hoop load path. It needs a doubler or thickened frame around it to carry the lost load; the corner needs a smooth radius because a sharp corner raises stress.

sections.h3: Tail unit loads into the rear fuselage

blocks.text: The tailplane carries a balancing load, often downward in steady level flight, and a manoeuvre load that can reverse direction. Treat the tailplane as a cantilever: its load times the distance to the fuselage gives a bending moment on the rear fuselage. That moment is largest at the tailplane root and falls toward the wing. The fin carries a side load from rudder deflection or sideslip. The fin bends as a cantilever and also twists about its span axis; the root joint must take both bending and torque. The fin spar and the fuselage frames that pick it up are sized by these root reactions.

The rear fuselage is therefore a beam under combined bending from tailplane and fin, plus cabin pressure if the pressure cabin extends that far. Near the fin root, skin and frames also see concentrated fitting loads. A common exam question gives a tailplane load and an arm; the answer is a bending moment at a station, then a stress using the fuselage section properties. Torsion of the closed section is covered in Unit 5; here keep to bending stress and joint reactions.

figure.caption: The tailplane load enters rear fuselage bending: through the fin root on a T-tail, or straight into rear fuselage frames on a conventional tail. Cabin pressure gives skin hoop stress; both meet at a combined stress check.

spec.title: Fuselage and tail load paths
spec.aria: Two branches, one from tailplane load into rear fuselage bending through the fin root on a T-tail or directly into frames on a conventional tail, and one from cabin pressure to skin hoop stress, meeting at a combined stress check.

examples.question: A fuselage has mean radius 1.2 m and skin thickness 1.6 mm. The cabin differential pressure is 55 kPa. At a section, the ultimate bending moment is 200 kN·m. The material is 2024 aluminium with yield about 345 MPa. Find the hoop stress, longitudinal pressure stress, second moment of area of the thin skin tube, bending stress at the outer fibre, total longitudinal stress on the tension side, and the von Mises stress there. Comment on the margin.
steps: Convert units: p = 55 kPa = 55 000 Pa; r = 1.2 m; t = 1.6 mm = 0.0016 m; M = 200 kN·m = 200 000 N·m.
Longitudinal pressure stress: σ_l,pressure = p r / (2t) = 55 000 × 1.2 / (2 × 0.0016) = 20 625 000 Pa = 20.625 MPa.
Second moment of area: I ≈ π r³ t = π × 1.2³ × 0.0016 = 8.686 × 10⁻³ m⁴.
Bending stress: σ_b = M y / I = (200 000 × 1.2) / (8.686 × 10⁻³) = 27.63 × 10⁶ Pa = 27.63 MPa. Here y = r = 1.2 m at the outer fibre.
Total longitudinal stress on the tension side: σ_l,total = 20.625 + 27.63 = 48.26 MPa.

The ultimate-load von Mises stress of 45.2 MPa is well below the ultimate strength of about 470 MPa. The limit-load stress is about two-thirds of this, well below the 345 MPa yield. Fatigue and buckling still need separate checks.
examples.answer: The tension-side longitudinal stress is 48.3 MPa and the von Mises stress is 45.2 MPa at ultimate load; both pass the ultimate strength check, and the limit-load stresses pass yield.
examples.check:
import math
p=55000
r=1.2
t=0.0016
M=200000
y=1.2
hoop=p*r/t/1e6
long=p*r/(2*t)/1e6
I=math.pi*r**3*t
bend=M*y/I/1e6
total=long+bend
vm=math.sqrt(total**2-total*hoop+hoop**2)
print(f'{hoop:.2f}')
print(f'{long:.3f}')
print(f'{I:.6f}')
print(f'{bend:.2f}')
print(f'{total:.2f}')
print(f'{vm:.2f}')

traps: Adding hoop stress straight into the longitudinal total. The two act at right angles and must be combined through von Mises or a principal stress check.
Using diameter instead of radius in p r / t. Hoop stress doubles if you slip in d where r belongs.

Using absolute cabin pressure instead of differential pressure. At 11 km altitude the outside pressure is only about 23 kPa, so a cabin held near 75 kPa absolute gives a differential of about 50–55 kPa — close to the full cabin pressure. At sea level the same cabin would give almost no differential at all.
Treating a thin fuselage tube as a solid circle. The thin-tube value is I ≈ π r³ t, not π r⁴ / 4.
Forgetting that bending changes sign around the section. One side is in tension, the other in compression, so the total longitudinal stress is different on each side.

quiz.q: State the two membrane stresses in a pressurised thin cylinder and their ratio.
quiz.a: Hoop stress σ_h = p r / t and longitudinal stress σ_l = p r / (2t); hoop stress is twice longitudinal stress.

quiz.q: Why is a fuselage window surround reinforced?
quiz.a: A window removes skin and breaks the hoop load path. A doubler or thickened frame carries the lost load and smooths the corner, reducing stress concentration.

quiz.q: A thin cylinder has mean radius 0.9 m, thickness 2 mm and differential pressure 60 kPa. Find the hoop stress and longitudinal stress.
A fuselage has r = 1.5 m, t = 2 mm, p = 50 kPa and M = 150 kN·m. Find the total longitudinal stress on the tension side.
Why is it wrong to add hoop stress directly to longitudinal stress?
quiz.a: They act on perpendicular faces, so they are a biaxial state, not two pulls on one line. A von Mises or principal stress combination accounts for their interaction; direct addition overestimates or misrepresents the failure condition.

quiz.q: A tailplane balancing load reverses from downward to upward. What changes in the rear fuselage stress?
quiz.a: The bending moment changes sign, so the tension and compression sides swap. Fatigue damage can grow on both sides over repeated reversals, so the load spectrum must include both directions.

quiz.q: What does a pressure bulkhead do?
quiz.a: It closes the pressurised cabin and converts cabin pressure into edge loads on the shell. A domed bulkhead carries pressure mainly by membrane action; a flat bulkhead bends.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, fuselage stress analysis is mostly done with finite element models of the idealised skin-stringer-frame assembly, with pressure and tail loads applied as load cases. Cut-outs are local submodels because a global mesh cannot resolve a window corner. Fatigue and damage tolerance then check the same stresses against repeated pressurisation cycles. Search for fuselage idealisation, cut-out reinforcement, fin root fitting load, and damage tolerance.
